ERC Furthers Initiatives Towards Implementing Open Access In Electricity

ERC Furthers Initiatives Towards Implementing Open Access In Electricity: Electricity Regulatory Commission Releases Two More Draft Directives For Stakeholder Comment

  • By
  • NEW SPOTLIGHT ONLINE
Sept. 15, 2026, 1:28 p.m.
  • share
  • tweet
  • Linkedin
  • Mail

The Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) is moving rapidly to implement open access in the electricity transmission and distribution system. With the aim of making Nepal's electricity sector competitive and ensuring the public's right to access quality, reliable, safe, and universally available electricity, the Commission has prioritized implementation of the Open Access Directive issued last Poush. Regarding the various draft directives related to open access, the Commission has stated that a subcommittee formed under the coordination of Commission member Mr. Lok Raj Pathak and comprising representatives of the Nepal Electricity Authority, the National Transmission Grid Company, and IPPAN, the umbrella organization of private power producers, has been working on the drafts with the participation of invited subject experts.

In this context, at its meeting held on 25 Bhadra 2083, the Electricity Regulatory Commission made public the drafts of two more open access-related directives, the Installation and Operation of Meters Directive, 2083, and the Deviation Settlement Mechanism and Related Matters Directive, 2083 for the opinions, suggestions, and comments of stakeholders and the general public. Concerned stakeholders and members of the public may submit their opinions, suggestions, and comments on the draft directives in writing to the Commission's office at Sano Gaucharan, Kathmandu, or by email to [email protected]. These directives are subordinate directives under Section 51 of the Directive on Open Access in the Electricity Transmission and Distribution System, 2082, and will be issued under Section 43 of the Electricity Regulatory Commission Act, 2074. With regard to the Commission's duties, functions, and powers, Section 14 of the Electricity Regulatory Commission Act, 2074, which concerns the maintenance of competition and the protection of consumer interests, empowers the Commission to make the arrangements necessary for open access in the electricity system. The Commission had already issued the Open Access Directive, 2082, in Poush of last year, and has now issued the drafts of two of the related directives required to bring that directive into full implementation.

Among the directives issued in draft form, the Installation and Operation of Meters Directive, 2083 sets out provisions on the location, type, and ownership of the special meters to be installed and operated for the fair, transparent, and effective implementation of open access, and establishes accuracy standards for energy measurement. It also makes arrangements to bring uniformity to meters installed across Nepal's electricity system, to ensure safety and quality standards, and to govern the collection, flow, management, and storage of data obtained from meters. In addition, it provides for the transmission and collection of meter data via Power Line Carrier, Radio Frequency, and GSM 3G/4G technologies, and for the management of this data through a central Meter Data Management System.

Likewise, the Deviation Settlement Mechanism and Related Matters Directive, 2083 proposes a mechanism for taking action on, and settling, deviations from pre-approved electricity import (drawal) and export (injection) schedules, to maintain the security, reliability, and stability of the electricity transmission and distribution system. Under the proposed directive, if an open access user's actual import or export of electricity differs from its scheduled import or export, a penalty (ranging from a minimum of Rs 4 to Rs 16 per unit) or an incentive (ranging from Rs 5 to Rs 20 per unit) will apply, depending on whether the deviation has a positive or negative effect on the grid. Open access users will receive the above penalty or incentive in proportion to the amount of power deviation, based on system frequency.

  1. What is the significance of the meters specified under the new directives for Nepal's power system in the context of open access?

Under open access, multiple generators and consumers are connected to the same transmission and distribution line, making it essential to measure, precisely and reliably, how much electricity each party has generated or consumed. Metering is therefore the backbone of open access. The accuracy-certified special meters prescribed under the new directive will:

● Measure each user's electricity generation and consumption data accurately and without dispute;

● Enable automatic collection, transmission, and storage of data through a Meter Data Management System;

● Allow data to be obtained even from remote meters, using technologies such as Power Line Carrier, Radio Frequency, and GSM 3G/4G; and

● Provide a transparent basis for calculating charges, penalties, and incentives.

Reliable metering is a precondition for the fair implementation of open access, which is why these directives are considered significant.

  1. What is “deviation” in a power system?

Every generator and buyer must submit a schedule in advance, indicating how much electricity it will generate, or how much it will consume, import, or export, during a given period. However, actual generation or consumption may turn out to be higher or lower than that scheduled amount, this difference is referred to as a “deviation.” For example, if a hydropower project schedules 100 MW of generation for the following day, but higher-than-expected water flow results in actual generation of 110 MW, the resulting 10 MW difference constitutes a deviation.

  1. Why is deviation management important in a power system?

A power system must continuously maintain a balance between generation and consumption; otherwise, system frequency will rise or fall, which can seriously affect grid stability and security and, in extreme cases, lead to blackouts. In an open access environment where multiple generators and buyers are connected simultaneously, even small individual deviations can accumulate and place significant stress on the grid. It is therefore essential to measure deviations promptly, identify their effect, positive or negative, on the grid, and apply penalties or incentives accordingly. Such a mechanism encourages users to adhere to their schedules as closely as possible, helps maintain system stability, and, over the long term, supports the development of a reliable and competitive electricity market.

The Commission has already issued, for the opinions, suggestions, and comments of stakeholders and the public, the drafts of two other open access-related directives (1)the Grievance Redress Directive, 2083, and (2) the Balancing and Settlement Directive, 2083. The Commission has stated that it is preparing to issue, in sequence, further directives necessary for open access implementation soon, including one to set transmission tariffs, as well as others such as a Grid Connectivity Directive, for the opinions, suggestions, and comments of stakeholders and the public. Individuals, organizations, and customers using the Nepal Electricity Authority's transmission and distribution system will also be able to avail themselves of open access.

At present, in the absence of open access provisions in Nepal, the Nepal Electricity Authority alone has had to bear the entire risk of the electricity market. However, once the Open Access Directive is fully implemented, any individual or organization generating or consuming electricity will no longer need to depend solely on the Nepal Electricity Authority. This is expected to reduce risk in the electricity market and to help build a competitive, predictable, and reliable electricity market.

The full text of the draft directives is available on the Commission's website, www.erc.gov.np .
